text: or dissem- inated disease, and all immunocompromised patients re- quire treatment.1 In immunocompetent patients, mild to moderate disease is treated with oral itraconazole; the duration of treatment is at least 6 months for pulmonary disease and 12 months for bone disease. Ketoconazole or fluconazole are less effec- tive alternatives (and ketoconazole is more toxic); the role of voriconazole or posaconazole is not clear, although they may be effective. Patients unable to tolerate azoles or in whom disease progresses should be switched to amphoter- icin B. Life-threatening disease (either pulmonary or ex- trapulmonary) should be treated intravenously with a lipid or conventional formulation of amphotericin B; patients are usually switched to oral itraconazole once stabilised. All patients with CNS disease should be given a lipid for- mulation of amphotericin B intravenously for 4 to 6 weeks, followed by an oral azole; the options for the latter include fluconazole, itraconazole, or voriconazole. Oral treatment should be continued for at least 12 months and until resolution of abnormalities in the CSF. In patients who are immunosuppressed, the recommended initial treatment is a lipid formulation of amphotericin B given intravenously for 1 to 2 weeks, or until improvement is noted. Once the patient has responded to this initial treat- ment they may be switched to oral itraconazole, which is continued until at least 12 months of therapy has been giv- en. Life-long itraconazole treatment may be needed in pa- tients in whom immunosuppression cannot be reversed, or in those who relapse despite appropriate therapy (a well- documented phenomenon in immunosuppressed patients). In pregnant patients presenting with blastomycosis a lipid formulation of amphotericin B is recommended; azoles should be avoided because of possible teratogenicity. If the neonate shows signs of infection, treatment with a conven- tional (deoxycholate) formulation of amphotericin B is recommended. Children may be treated with amphotericin B or oral itraconazole, depending on the severity of infec- tion; in general, they tolerate conventional amphotericin B better than adults, and lipid formulations may not be need- ed. 1.
